subject: physics

moments.title: Tycho's island observatory
moments.body: Funded by the Danish king with an entire island, Tycho builds the largest, most precise observatory in the world — accurate to 1/60 of a degree, all done by naked eye. He observes the heavens for 25 years before quarrelling with the new king and moving to Prague.
moments.takeaway: A nobleman, a metal nose (lost in a duel) and the most precise pre-telescopic observations ever made.

moments.title: Kepler joins Tycho
moments.body: Kepler — a Lutheran refugee, mathematician, mystic — becomes Tycho's assistant. Tycho dies the next year, allegedly of a bladder rupture from politeness at a long dinner. Kepler inherits the data.
moments.takeaway: The richest astronomical dataset of the era passes to a poor mystic mathematician.

moments.title: Three laws
moments.body: Kepler spends 8 years on Mars alone. The orbit is an ellipse, not a circle. He formulates three laws: orbits are ellipses; equal areas in equal times; T^2 proportional to a^3. He believes the cosmos is musical and Platonic; he discovers physics anyway.
moments.takeaway: Empirical laws of planetary motion, derived from one obsessive analysis of Mars.

moments.title: Newton derives Kepler
moments.body: Newton shows Kepler's three empirical laws follow from a single inverse-square gravitational force. The two-body problem is solved exactly.
moments.takeaway: Kepler's three laws are unified into one — Newton's gravity.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Kepler's laws underpin all orbital mechanics — satellites, interplanetary probes, exoplanet detection. NASA's Kepler space telescope (named after him) found 2,600 exoplanets by transit photometry.
now.open_questions: How accurately can we determine masses of multi-planet systems from Kepler-style timing?

reflection: Kepler believed the cosmos was musical and Platonic. His mysticism led him to seek patterns — and find real laws. When does pseudoscience accidentally produce science?
